justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing level at the time of the forecast, likely around 85–86 for the underlying asset or index in question. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to recent price action and short-term momentum, expecting minimal deviation from the current trend, hence a point estimate of 86.1. Over one week, I incorporated a slight continuation of that trend while acknowledging mean-reversion pressures, landing at 86.5. At one month, the estimate of 87.0 reflects a gentle bullish tilt consistent with a modest trending environment, though the directional conviction weakens considerably as the horizon extends.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the narrow band of roughly ±1.9 points captures typical intraday and overnight volatility, drawing on recent realized volatility measures and the expectation that no major scheduled events would dramatically reprice the asset. At one week, the interval widens to ±4 points, incorporating the possibility of mid-week data releases, sentiment shifts, or technical breakdowns that could accumulate. At one month, the ±8 point band reflects the full range of macro developments, earnings cycles, and structural shifts in positioning that can materialize over a 30-day period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes beyond the stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from a major central bank, an unexpectedly strong economic data print, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could drive prices well above the upper bounds. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode triggered by credit stress, an inflation shock, or a geopolitical escalation could break decisively below the lower bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves in either direction, particularly around month-end or holiday periods.

It is worth noting that these intervals represent 90% confidence bands, meaning there is still a 10% probability mass in the tails. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that truly extreme outcomes — think a flash crash, a black swan macro event, or a sudden regulatory shock — carry more probability weight than a normal distribution would suggest. Forecasters who treat these intervals as hard bounds are likely to be surprised more frequently than once in ten observations.
